name: Powdered pearl
lead: Powdered pearl, or pearl powder, is finely ground pearl or nacre (mother-of-pearl), composed mainly of calcium carbonate with an organic protein matrix. It is a traditional Chinese medicine ingredient used for roughly two thousand years, and it is applied to the skin or taken by mouth for complexion and general health.[1][2]

In appearance contexts it is promoted as a skin-brightening and anti-ageing ingredient. Published research is mostly laboratory, animal and biomaterials work on wound healing and bone repair, plus a few small human studies of other outcomes; a narrative review describes the evidence base as lacking in-depth understanding despite the long history of use.[2] No trial of pearl powder for complexion or skin lightening appears in the sources reviewed.
infobox: Topical masks and creams; oral powder or capsules

paras: Pearl powder is made by grinding pearls into small grains, whereas nacre powder comes from the inner shell layer. Pearls form when an irritant lodges in an oyster and is coated with nacre.[3] The mineral phase is mainly calcium carbonate, held in a framework of organic molecules including water-soluble matrix proteins, which researchers consider important to its biological activity.[1][3] Nacre and pearl extracts are more commonly reported than pearl itself because pearls are expensive and limited in supply.[3]

In traditional Chinese medicine pearl is credited with calming the mind, clearing the eyes and detoxifying the muscle, and pearl powder is used for beauty care as well as health indications.[2][3] A 2021 review lists wound healing, bone repair and treatment of skin conditions among its emerging biomedical applications.[2]
No studies found testing pearl powder for skin brightening or complexion in humans. Human research on pearl-derived products addresses other outcomes.

A randomised, placebo-controlled trial of protein-rich pearl powder examined antioxidant status in a small group of volunteers, alongside laboratory work.[4] A pilot randomised trial gave bio-calcium from Pinctada maxima shell to postmenopausal women with reduced bone mineral density,[5] and a study assessed calcium bioavailability of nano-sized pearl powder in adults.[6] A case report described a 94-year-old woman with a stage 2 pressure injury treated with a metronidazole and nano pearl powder mixture.[7] Two registered trials compare pearl powder with CPP-ACP for enamel white spot lesions.[8][9]

Most remaining work is preclinical. A 2026 narrative review found pearl-specific studies generally support osteogenic activity in cell, scaffold and defect models, while noting heterogeneity and limited direct evidence on high-dose toxicity or heavy-metal risk.[10]

A 2026 review notes that pearl-specific literature offers limited direct evidence on chronic biosafety, immunogenicity or heavy-metal-related risk of nano-pearl powder.[10] No safety data for cosmetic or oral use for complexion appear in the sources reviewed.

card.summary: Ground pearl used in Chinese medicine for a luminous complexion; research covers wound and bone repair, not skin brightening.
card.note: No human trials for skin brightening; long-term safety data are limited.

quick.overview:
Powdered pearl is finely ground pearl or mother-of-pearl, a traditional Chinese medicine used for over two thousand years in beauty and health preparations. It is sold as a topical mask ingredient and as an oral powder.

Modern research mostly covers wound healing and bone repair in laboratory and animal models, with a few small human studies on other outcomes. No trial tests it for complexion or skin brightening.
quick.mechanism: Pearl is mostly calcium carbonate with a protein matrix. Researchers attribute antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and tissue-repair activity mainly to the water-soluble matrix proteins, studied in cells and animals.
quick.risks: Reviews say direct evidence on long-term safety, heavy-metal content and immune effects is limited. No safety data specific to cosmetic use appear in the sources reviewed.
